newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Euro shares weighed down by Wall St, politics.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Euro shares weighed down by Wall St, politics.

text.p: European bourses fell in thin trade on Friday, with investors rattled by a poor overnight close on Wall Street and a bout of jitters over political uncertainty.
On currency markets, the dollar weakened slightly against the yen as the suspension of a major Japanese insurer prompted speculation about higher interest rates in Tokyo.

London and Paris, both facing general elections in coming weeks, chalked up early losses but Frankfurt fell more sharply, depressed by New York's weaker bonds and stocks, which fell 20.47 points to 6,792.25 on Thursday on the Dow Jones industrial average.
"Everything's just looking a little tired and Friday-like," said one dealer.

Doubts about the outcome of Britain's May 1 general election and increasing likelihood of interest rate rises soon after dampened prices and activity. Stronger-than-expected growth figures did little to help.

"The figures mean four percent annualised growth which is pretty strong growth, well above trend and reinforces the likelihood of rate increases soon," said Credit Lyonnais Laing economist, Andrew Smith.
Many investors were sitting on the sidelines ahead of the poll in which the Conservative government is expected to be ousted by the oppostion Labour party, according to opinion polls.
The Paris bourse fell nearly 0.5 percent by lunchtime but volume was thin with many investors were holding back amid election uncertainty, traders said.

"Investors will steer clear until the election. The risk, in terms of market valuation, is too great. Better wait a month and find out what France's direction will be," said one trader. "Until then, we'll be driven by the polls."
An IPSOS poll showing the ruling conservative coalition would get a wafer-thin majority weighed on French financial markets on Thursday afternoon.
Frankfurt had the worst day, falling nearly 0.7 percent in floor trading and in computerised dealing as investors, depressed by Wall Street, pocketed profits before the weekend.

In currencies, the dollar was virtually unchanged on the mark but slipped slightly against the yen, with dollar sentiment hit by a rise in Japanese market interest rates overnight because of renewed worries over Japan's financial industry.

The worries were prompted by the suspension of the big Japanese insurance company Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Company. This triggered concern that Nissan's foreign bonds would be liquidated, causing a large repatriation of funds.
But the slide was slight and the dollar was not expected to move much before the weekend meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from the G7 group of industrialised countries in Washington.

"The latest worries about Japan's financial system are a distraction for the market ahead of the G7, and the yen is a touch stronger as a result but the FX impact was marginal," said Roger Francis, senior analyst at IBJ International.
The dollar was also supported against the yen by a comment from Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita who said the central bank was sticking to its easy monetary policy for the time being.
Traders will be keeping a close on eye on Friday's meeting in Washington between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
STOCKS AT 1100 GMT
London's FTSE 100 was down 13.0 points at 4,375.0.
The Paris CAC-40 index fell 9.66 points at 2,530.17.
Frankfurt's DAX index was down 21.33 at 3,376.31.
CURRENCIES AT 1100 GMT
The dollar stood at 1.7160 against the mark versus 1.7150 in late European trade on Thursday. Against the yen, the dollar was quoted at 125.65 from 125.90.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $341.35 an ounce after ending at $340.65 in London. Silver was at $4.73, one cent higher.
